questions.q:
Match each finding about a place in Column I with what the chapter says should follow from it in Column II.
Column I: 1. The place has many young children  2. The proportion of the elderly in the population is higher  3. There is a higher proportion of young working-age people  4. A firm studies the age, gender and income of its potential customers
Column II: P. More facilities for healthcare are required  Q. Products are created to match people's needs  R. More schools are needed  S. A greater need for gainful employment generation
Choose the correct matching.
questions.a: 1-R, 2-P, 3-S, 4-Q: many young children means more schools are needed; a higher proportion of elderly means more healthcare facilities; a higher proportion of young working-age people means a greater need for gainful employment generation; and businesses use age, gender and income to create products that match people's needs.

questions.q: (a) Define demography as the chapter does. (b) Name the three components of demography shown in Fig. 6.2.
questions.a: (a) Demography is the study of the composition of human population in terms of different factors like age, sex, occupation and religion, and how they change over time. (b) Size; pattern and trend; and structure and composition.
s: (a) Defines demography as the study of the composition of the human population by factors such as age, sex, occupation and religion, and how it changes over time
(b) Names all three components: size, pattern and trend, and structure and composition

questions.q: Answer briefly. (a) What is a census, in the chapter's words? (b) How often is the census generally conducted in India? (c) Name any three kinds of information the census collects from individuals.
questions.a: (a) A census is the official count of people living in a country in a particular period; the margin calls it the process of collecting, compiling, analysing and disseminating demographic, economic and social information of all persons in a country or a well-defined part of it at a specific time. (b) Generally every 10 years. (c) Any three of: age, gender, marital status, educational levels, languages spoken, religion, family size, occupation, employment status and income levels.
s: (a) States that a census is the official count of the people living in a country in a particular period (or the margin definition)
(b) Every 10 years
(c) Any three correct items from the chapter's list, such as age, marital status, languages spoken, occupation or income levels

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the census as the chapter describes it.
I. It collects demographic, economic and social information of all persons in a country or a well-defined part of a country at a specific time.
II. Among other things, it records the languages a person speaks and his or her employment status.
III. Because it is an official count, it records only the total number of people and not their characteristics.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and II only. The census collects information on age, gender, marital status, education, languages spoken, religion, family size, occupation, employment status and income, so it records people's characteristics as well as their number; statement III is wrong.

questions.q: A gram panchayat's report on Rampur village (illustrative) contains three findings. (i) 'Rampur has 4,260 residents.' (ii) 'Rampur's population has risen at every census since 1991, but more slowly each time.' (iii) 'About a third of Rampur's residents are under 15, and most adults work on farms.' Fig. 6.2 names three components of demography: size; pattern and trend; and structure and composition. Place each finding under one component and say what in the finding tells you so.
questions.a: (i) Size: it tells how many people live in the village. (ii) Pattern and trend: it describes how the population has changed over time. (iii) Structure and composition: it describes how the population is made up by age and by occupation.
s: (i) Size, because it gives only the number of people
(ii) Pattern and trend, because it describes change in the population over time
(iii) Structure and composition, because it describes the make-up of the people by age and occupation

questions.q:
The municipal office of a small town in Madhya Pradesh studies its latest population figures. Of the town's 50,000 people, 15,000 are children under 15, 31,000 are aged 15 to 64 and 4,000 are older than 64. Many young adults complain that they cannot find work in the town. A shopkeeper who is opening a new store also asks the office for the figures, to decide what to stock.
(a) The chapter's margin note gives the age band of the working-age population. How many people in the town are of working age?
(b) What percentage of the town's people are children under 15?
(c) Which planning need does the chapter link with a higher proportion of young working-age people?
(d) Name two characteristics of customers that, according to the chapter, businesses assess, which the shopkeeper could use.
questions.a: (a) The working-age population is 15 to 64 years, so 31,000 people. (b) 15,000 out of 50,000 = 30 per cent. (c) A greater need for gainful employment generation. (d) Any two of age, gender and income.
s: (a) 31,000, using the 15 to 64 band
(c) Gainful employment generation (creating jobs)
(d) Any two of age, gender and income

questions.q: Two wards of Jaipur (illustrative figures) each have 40,000 people. Ward A has 12,800 people under 15, 24,800 aged 15 to 64 and 2,400 above 64. Ward B has 6,000 under 15, 25,200 aged 15 to 64 and 8,800 above 64. This year the city can fund one new primary school and one new health centre, and must put them in different wards. (a) Find the percentage of each ward's people who are under 15 and who are above 64. (b) Using the chapter's planning rules, decide which ward should get the school and which the health centre, giving a reason for each. (c) A company wants to open a shop selling toys and children's books in one of the wards. Which ward should it choose, and which customer characteristic named in the chapter does that choice rest on?
questions.a: (a) Ward A: 12,800 / 40,000 = 32 per cent under 15 and 2,400 / 40,000 = 6 per cent above 64. Ward B: 6,000 / 40,000 = 15 per cent under 15 and 8,800 / 40,000 = 22 per cent above 64. (b) The school goes to Ward A, because the chapter says a place with many young children needs more schools, and A's share of children (32 per cent) is more than twice B's. The health centre goes to Ward B, because a higher proportion of elderly means more healthcare facilities are required, and B's elderly share (22 per cent) is far above A's 6 per cent. (c) Ward A, because it has far more children; the choice rests on age, one of the characteristics (age, gender, income) businesses use to match products to people's needs.
s: (a) Ward A: 32 per cent under 15 and 6 per cent above 64
(a) Ward B: 15 per cent under 15 and 22 per cent above 64
(b) School to Ward A, with the rule that many young children means more schools are needed
(b) Health centre to Ward B, with the rule that a higher proportion of elderly means more healthcare facilities
(c) Ward A, resting on the age of customers

questions.q: In 2023 India became the world's most populous country. Which country did it surpass to do so?
questions.a: China. The chapter says that in 2023 India surpassed China to become the world's most populous country.

questions.q: Fig. 6.3 gives the population in 2024 of India as 144 crore and of the United States as 33 crore. By how many crore did India's population exceed that of the United States?
questions.a: 111 crore, because 144 - 33 = 111.

questions.q: Fig. 6.3 lists the ten most populous countries of 2024, among them India, China, Pakistan and Nigeria. Which of the following correctly names one of these ten that the chapter says is already seeing a shrinking population, and one that it says continues to grow rapidly?
o: China is shrinking; Nigeria continues to grow rapidly
India is shrinking; China continues to grow rapidly
China is shrinking; India continues to grow rapidly
Nigeria is shrinking; China continues to grow rapidly
questions.a: China is shrinking; Nigeria continues to grow rapidly. The chapter names China, Japan and Italy as already shrinking and Nigeria and Ethiopia as continuing to grow rapidly; India's population is described only as 'growing for now'.

questions.q: World population grew rapidly from the 1950s onwards. (a) Name any two medical advancements of this period that the chapter mentions. (b) Name the two diseases from which deaths of children came down in this period.
questions.a: (a) Any two of: the use of antibiotics, vaccines and oral rehydration solution. (b) Malaria and diarrhoea.
s: (a) Any two of antibiotics, vaccines and oral rehydration solution
(b) Malaria and diarrhoea

questions.q: True or False? 'According to Fig. 6.5, India's population in 2025 (1,460 million) was more than four times its population in 1951 (361 million).' Give the verdict and show the working.
questions.a: True. Four times 361 million is 1,444 million, and 1,460 million is more than that (1,460 / 361 is about 4.04).
s: Verdict: True
Working: 4 x 361 = 1,444 million, which is less than 1,460 million

questions.q:
Assertion (A): World population grew rapidly from the 1950s onwards.
Reason (R): From the 1950s, better water and sanitation facilities became available to more people, and deaths of children due to malaria and diarrhoea came down.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. The chapter links the rapid growth from the 1950s to fewer deaths, brought about by better water and sanitation, medical advances and fewer child deaths from malaria and diarrhoea.

questions.q:
A Class 8 group in Lucknow is making a wall chart called 'India in the World, 2025'. They take these figures from the chapter: the world's population in 2025 was 8.2 billion; Asia held 4.8 billion of these people and Africa 1.5 billion (Fig. 6.6); and India had 1,460 million people (Fig. 6.5). Take 1 billion = 1,000 million.
(a) Express India's population in billions.
(b) Find India's share of the world's population, to the nearest whole per cent, and say whether it fits the chapter's statement about the share of Indians in the world.
(c) Find, to the nearest whole per cent, what share of Asia's people live in India.
(d) One member wants the chart's headline to read 'Asia will always hold most of the world's people'. Using what the chapter says about growth in different countries, should the chart print this headline? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) 1,460 million = 1.46 billion. (b) 1.46 / 8.2 x 100 = about 17.8, or 18 per cent, which is close to the chapter's statement that Indians are around 17 per cent of the world population. (c) 1.46 / 4.8 x 100 = about 30 per cent. (d) It should not print 'always'. In 2025 Asia did hold most people (4.8 of 8.2 billion, about 59 per cent), but the chapter gives no projection by region, and it says China and Japan in Asia are already shrinking while African nations such as Nigeria and Ethiopia continue to grow rapidly, so Asia's share may fall. A safe headline is 'In 2025 Asia held more than half the world's people'.
s: (a) 1.46 billion
(b) About 18 per cent (17.8), close to the chapter's 'around 17 per cent'
(c) About 30 per cent of Asia's people
(d) Rejects 'always': Asia held most people in 2025, but China and Japan are shrinking while Nigeria and Ethiopia grow rapidly, so the share can change

questions.q: (a) Using Fig. 6.5, find the increase in India's population from 1971 (548 million) to 1981 (683 million). (b) Express this increase in crore (1 crore = 10 million).
questions.a: (a) 683 - 548 = 135 million. (b) 135 million / 10 = 13.5 crore.
s: (a) Increase of 135 million
(b) 13.5 crore

questions.q: In which form does the chapter say the birth rate is usually stated?
o: Live human births per 1,000 population in a year
Children a woman has over her whole lifetime
Deaths per 1,000 people in a year
Live births per 100 married couples in ten years
questions.a: As the total number of live human births per 1,000 population in a year.

questions.q: According to the chapter, what follows when many babies are being born in a country?
o: The birth rate is high and the population will grow faster
The death rate is high and the population will shrink
The population becomes stable at once
questions.a: The birth rate is high and the population will grow faster.

questions.q: District X records 18 live births per 1,000 people in a year and District Y records 21. An officer concludes that women in District Y have more children over their lifetimes than women in District X. Which indicator from Fig. 6.7 would she actually need to check this conclusion?
questions.a: The fertility rate, because it is the average number of children a woman would have in her lifetime; the figures she has are birth rates, which count births per 1,000 of the whole population in a year.

questions.q: Name the four key indicators of demography given in Fig. 6.7.
questions.a: Birth rate, fertility rate, death or mortality rate, and migration.
s: Names any two of the four indicators correctly
Names the other two, so that all four (birth rate, fertility rate, death or mortality rate, migration) are given

questions.q: True or False? 'If women in a country start having fewer children, the country's birth rate stays the same as long as the number of women does not change.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. The chapter says that when fertility rates fall, because women have fewer children, the birth rate also drops, and this slows down population growth.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: when fertility falls (women have fewer children) the birth rate also drops, slowing growth

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A fertility rate of 2.1 is called the replacement level fertility rate.
Reason (R): It is the number of children needed to replace the parents in the population.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. The chapter says 2.1 is called the replacement level fertility rate because it is the number of children needed to replace the parents.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements.
I. If fewer babies are being born, a population might grow slowly or even start shrinking over time.
II. The fertility rate is measured as the number of live births per 1,000 population in a year.
III. If the fertility rate is below 2.1, the population might shrink over time.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only. Statement II describes the birth rate; the fertility rate is the average number of children a woman would have in her lifetime.

questions.q: Three villages report these yearly figures per 1,000 people (illustrative). Village X: 24 births, 10 deaths, nobody moves in or out. Village Y: 14 births, 9 deaths, 12 people leave to work in cities and nobody arrives. Village Z: 12 births, 13 deaths, 6 people arrive and nobody leaves. (a) For each village, find births minus deaths per 1,000. (b) For each village, find the overall change per 1,000 once migration is included. (c) Which village's population is falling, and which of the four key indicators is responsible? (d) A block officer says Village Z must be shrinking because its deaths are more than its births. Judge his statement.
questions.a: (a) X: 24 - 10 = +14; Y: 14 - 9 = +5; Z: 12 - 13 = -1. (b) X: +14; Y: +5 - 12 = -7; Z: -1 + 6 = +5. (c) Village Y is falling, by 7 per 1,000 a year, because of migration out of it, even though its births are more than its deaths. (d) He is wrong. Z loses 1 per 1,000 through births and deaths but gains 6 through migrants arriving, so it grows by 5 per 1,000. The chapter says a population results from births, deaths and the movement of people in and out together, not from births and deaths alone.
s: (a) Births minus deaths: X +14, Y +5, Z -1 per 1,000
(b) Overall change: X +14, Y -7, Z +5 per 1,000
(c) Village Y is falling, because of migration (people leaving)
(d) Rejects the officer's claim: Z grows by 5 per 1,000 because arrivals outweigh the excess of deaths; births, deaths and migration act together

questions.q: In which year did China introduce its One-Child Policy?
questions.a: 1979. The Chinese government introduced the One-Child Policy in 1979.

questions.q: What did India's 'Hum do humare do' campaign, run from 1952 onwards, emphasise?
o: Not having more than two children
Having only one child in each family
Allowing up to three children in each family
questions.a: It emphasised not having more than two children.

questions.q: Fig. 6.11 gives the fertility rate and the literacy rate among women for six states: Bihar 3.0 and 55 per cent; Uttar Pradesh 2.4 and 66.1 per cent; Jharkhand 2.3 and 61.7 per cent; Karnataka 1.7 and 73.4 per cent; Punjab 1.6 and 79.4 per cent; Delhi 1.6 and 83.7 per cent. (a) Which of these states have a fertility rate above the replacement level of 2.1? (b) Among those states, which has the highest literacy rate among women, and is that rate higher or lower than the rate of every state below replacement level?
questions.a: (a) Bihar (3.0), Uttar Pradesh (2.4) and Jharkhand (2.3). (b) Uttar Pradesh, with 66.1 per cent, which is lower than the rate of each state below replacement level: Karnataka 73.4, Punjab 79.4 and Delhi 83.7 per cent.
s: (a) Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and Jharkhand
(b) Uttar Pradesh at 66.1 per cent, lower than Karnataka, Punjab and Delhi

questions.q: Answer these questions on China's One-Child Policy. (a) Why did the Chinese government introduce it? (b) What happened to families who broke the rule? (c) In which year did China end the policy, and how many children does it now allow?
questions.a: (a) In the 1970s the government was worried that its fast-growing population would cause shortages of food, jobs and housing. (b) They faced fines or job loss. (c) China ended the policy in 2015 and now allows up to three children.
s: (a) Fear that a fast-growing population would cause shortages of food, jobs and housing
(b) Fines or job loss
(c) Ended in 2015; up to three children now allowed

questions.q:
Match each fertility rate in Column I with what it describes in Column II, as the chapter gives the figures.
Column I: 1. 7.5  2. 1  3. 5.7  4. 1.9
Column II: P. India's fertility rate in 1950  Q. China's fertility rate in 1963  R. India's fertility rate in 2025  S. China's fertility rate in 2025
Choose the correct matching.
questions.a: 1-Q, 2-S, 3-P, 4-R: China's fertility rate fell from 7.5 in 1963 to 1 in 2025, and India's fell from 5.7 in 1950 to 1.9 in 2025.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The share of China's population above 65 years is expected to rise from 14 per cent in 2023 to 26 per cent in 2050.
Reason (R): China ended its One-Child Policy in 2015 and now allows up to three children.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. The chapter links the rising elderly share to people living longer due to access to better healthcare; ending the policy in 2015 does not explain why the population is growing older.

questions.q: True or False? 'The One-Child Policy changed only the size of China's population; it did not change family life.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. The chapter says the policy had a far-reaching impact on households and society: a whole generation of children do not have siblings and kinship networks, the web of relationships through blood, marriage and adoption.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: a whole generation of children grew up without siblings and kinship networks, a far-reaching impact on households and society

questions.q:
A voluntary group working in villages of Jharkhand reads Fig. 6.11, which gives Jharkhand a fertility rate of 2.3 and a literacy rate among women of 61.7 per cent, and Karnataka a fertility rate of 1.7 and a literacy rate among women of 73.4 per cent. The group has money for only one project this year: scholarships to keep village girls in school, or a poster and radio campaign about small families, like India's earlier 'Hum do humare do' campaign.
(a) Is Jharkhand's fertility rate above or below the replacement level, and what does the chapter say this means for its population?
(b) By how many percentage points is Jharkhand's literacy rate among women lower than Karnataka's?
(c) Name two causes of falling fertility given on page 175 that the scholarship project would work on.
(d) Which project would you advise the group to fund? Justify your choice using the chapter's evidence.
questions.a: (a) Above the replacement level of 2.1, so its population is likely to grow. (b) 73.4 - 61.7 = 11.7 percentage points. (c) Better access to quality education, especially among girls; and women getting formal education and working in formal jobs, so they marry later and have fewer children. (d) Either choice can be defended if it uses the evidence. For scholarships: the chapter names girls' education as one important factor in falling fertility, and in Fig. 6.11 the states with higher literacy among women have lower fertility. For the campaign: India's fertility fell from 5.7 in 1950 to 1.9 in 2025 in a period that included campaigns like 'Hum do humare do'. A good answer notes that education works through later marriage and formal jobs, which the chapter explains, while it gives no measure of what the campaign alone achieved.
s: (a) Above 2.1, so the population is likely to grow
(b) 11.7 percentage points
(c) Girls' education, and women in formal education and formal jobs marrying later and having fewer children
(d) A justified choice that uses the chapter's evidence (girls' education as a cause and the Fig. 6.11 pattern, or the campaign and India's fall from 5.7 to 1.9)

questions.q: According to the chapter, what does a lower mortality rate in a country indicate?
o: The availability of quality healthcare and better nutrition
A rise in the number of babies born each year
A large number of migrants arriving in the country
A fertility rate above the replacement level
questions.a: It indicates the availability of quality healthcare and better nutrition among the people of the country.

questions.q: Which cities does the chapter name as having experienced significant population growth due to migration?
questions.a: Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru.

questions.q: (a) What is child mortality, as the chapter defines it? (b) Give India's child mortality in 1950 and in 2023.
questions.a: (a) The number of deaths of children under 5 years of age per 1,000 live births. (b) 271 per 1,000 in 1950 and 28 per 1,000 in 2023.
s: (a) Deaths of children under 5 years of age per 1,000 live births
(b) 271 in 1950 and 28 in 2023 (per 1,000 live births)

questions.q: Answer briefly. (a) What is life expectancy, in the chapter's meaning? (b) What was India's life expectancy at birth at independence, and what was it in 2024? (c) Give the reason the chapter gives for life expectancy in India being low, around 30 to 35 years, in the 1950s.
questions.a: (a) The average number of years a newborn is expected to live if it grows up with the same health, safety and living conditions that people in its country have today. (b) 30 years at independence and 70 years in 2024. (c) Healthcare and nutrition were not as good then.
s: (a) Average years a newborn is expected to live under today's health, safety and living conditions
(b) 30 years at independence and 70 years in 2024
(c) Healthcare and nutrition were not as good

questions.q: True or False? 'A city whose own birth rate is low can still see its population rise over time if many migrants keep arriving there.' Give the verdict and the reason from the chapter.
questions.a: True. The chapter says areas witnessing an influx of migrants see a rise in population over time; Delhi, Mumbai and Bengaluru have grown significantly because of migration.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: areas with an influx of migrants see their population rise over time (example: Delhi, Mumbai or Bengaluru)

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The concentration of a very large population in a limited area can strain services like transportation and housing.
Reason (R): The chapter says natural disasters and political instability are the only reasons people migrate.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false. The chapter says people tend to migrate for better employment opportunities, education and so on; natural disasters and political instability are only reasons that sometimes push people to move.

questions.q:
A district health report from Odisha (illustrative figures) says: 'In 2005 the district recorded 9,000 live births, and 540 children under 5 years of age died. In 2023 it recorded 8,000 live births, and 160 children under 5 died. Over these years the district opened new health centres and ran a nutrition programme for mothers and infants.'
(a) Find the district's child mortality in 2005, as the chapter measures it.
(b) Find the district's child mortality in 2023.
(c) Compare the 2023 figure with India's child mortality of 28 in 2023, and say what, by the chapter, a lower mortality figure indicates.
(d) The report's author wants to add: 'So the district's life expectancy has now reached 70 years.' Can the data above support that sentence? Give a reason using the chapter's meaning of life expectancy.
questions.a: (a) 540 / 9,000 x 1,000 = 60 per 1,000 live births. (b) 160 / 8,000 x 1,000 = 20 per 1,000 live births. (c) The district's 20 is lower than India's 28, which by the chapter indicates the availability of quality healthcare and better nutrition. (d) No. Life expectancy is the average number of years a newborn is expected to live under today's health, safety and living conditions, so it depends on deaths at all ages; the data count only deaths of children under 5, so they show survival is improving but cannot fix a life expectancy of 70.
s: (a) 60 per 1,000 live births
(b) 20 per 1,000 live births
(c) Lower than India's 28; indicates quality healthcare and better nutrition
(d) No: life expectancy depends on living conditions and deaths at every age, while the data cover only deaths under 5

questions.q: According to the chapter, from when did India's fertility rate begin declining, so that it is now below replacement level?
questions.a: After the mid-1980s.

questions.q: Why does a country's population grow rapidly in Stage 2 of demographic transition?
o: The death rate falls while the birth rate stays high
The birth rate and the death rate both fall together
The birth rate rises while the death rate stays high
The death rate stays low while the birth rate falls
questions.a: Because the death rate falls, with better healthcare, while the birth rate stays high.

questions.q: Demographers have observed that populations go through transitions. Name any four influences on these transitions that the chapter gives.
questions.a: Economic development, improved healthcare, education, and increased participation of women in decision making in the household.
s: Names any two of: economic development, improved healthcare, education, women's increased participation in household decision making
Names the remaining two, giving all four

questions.q: Describe each of the three stages of demographic transition in one line, saying what happens to the birth rate and the death rate and to population growth.
questions.a: Stage 1: both the birth rate and the death rate are high, so population growth is very slow or stagnant. Stage 2: the death rate falls but the birth rate stays high, so the population grows rapidly. Stage 3: the death rate is low and the birth rate begins to fall, so overall population growth slows.
s: Stage 1: high birth and high death rates, growth very slow or stagnant
Stage 2: death rate falls, birth rate still high, rapid growth
Stage 3: death rate low, birth rate falls, growth slows

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In Stage 1 of demographic transition, a country's population grows rapidly.
Reason (R): In Stage 1, both the birth rate and the death rate are high.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is false, but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true. In Stage 1 the birth and death rates are both high, so population growth is very slow or stagnant; rapid growth comes in Stage 2.

questions.q: Ishaan says: 'India's fertility rate has fallen below the replacement level, so India's population has already started to shrink, just like the populations of Italy and Japan.' Test his claim against the chapter. Say what he has got right and what he has got wrong.
questions.a: Partly right. Right: the chapter says India's fertility rate began declining after the mid-1980s and is now below replacement level (1.9 in 2025). Wrong: the chapter says India's population is still growing for now; a population starts to shrink in Stage 3 only if fertility drops significantly and births become even lower, as in Italy, Japan and South Korea, which India has not yet reached.
s: Verdict: partly right
Confirms the right part: India's fertility is now below replacement level (1.9 in 2025)
Corrects the wrong part: India's population is still growing; shrinking comes only when fertility drops significantly, as in Italy and Japan

questions.q: Country M (an imaginary country) is described at three dates. In 1920 most families have six or seven children, but many children die young; there are few hospitals and few people can read. In 1965 vaccines, clean water and hospitals have reached most towns and far fewer people die young, but families still have five or six children. In 2015 most girls finish school, many women work in offices, cities are growing and costly to live in, families have one or two children, and deaths remain low. (a) Name the stage of demographic transition Country M is in at each date, with the clue that shows it. (b) At which of the three dates was the population growing fastest? Explain using the birth and death rates. (c) Say what would have to happen next for Country M's population to start shrinking, and name one country where the chapter says this is already seen.
questions.a: (a) 1920: Stage 1, because both births and deaths are high (many children born, many die young, poor healthcare and low literacy). 1965: Stage 2, because deaths have fallen with better healthcare while families still have many children. 2015: Stage 3, because deaths stay low and births have fallen with education, women in the workforce, urbanisation and a high cost of living. (b) In 1965, because the death rate had fallen while the birth rate was still high, which the chapter says causes rapid growth. (c) Fertility would have to drop significantly, leading to even lower births; the chapter says this is seen in Italy, Japan and South Korea.
s: (a) 1920: Stage 1, high births and high deaths
(a) 1965: Stage 2, deaths fallen but births still high
(a) 2015: Stage 3, deaths low and births falling
(b) 1965, because the death rate had fallen while the birth rate stayed high
(c) Fertility drops significantly, giving even lower births; example Italy, Japan or South Korea

questions.q: India's sex ratio was 933 in Census 2001 and 943 in Census 2011. By how much did it improve?
questions.a: By 10 females per 1,000 males, because 943 - 933 = 10.

questions.q: (a) What does the chapter call characteristics such as the age, gender, occupation and education of a population? (b) Name the key demographic indicator that population composition uses to measure gender balance.
questions.a: (a) The structure of the population, or population composition. (b) The sex ratio, the number of females per 1,000 males.
s: (a) Structure of the population or population composition
(b) Sex ratio

questions.q: Answer briefly about India's population pyramid. (a) What shape did it have in the 1950s? (b) What shape does it have in recent years? (c) Why has its base become narrower?
questions.a: (a) A narrow triangle, with many children and young people and fewer older people. (b) Less like a triangle and more bell-shaped. (c) Because families are having fewer children than before.
s: (a) A narrow triangle
(b) Bell-shaped
(c) Families are having fewer children

questions.q:
Match each figure in Column I with what it describes in Column II, as the chapter gives it.
Column I: 1. 943  2. 933  3. 48.5 per cent  4. 16 per cent
Column II: P. India's sex ratio in Census 2001  Q. Women's share of India's total population in 2011  R. Uttar Pradesh's share of India's population (Fig. 6.13)  S. India's sex ratio in Census 2011
Choose the correct matching.
questions.a: 1-S, 2-P, 3-Q, 4-R: the sex ratio was 933 in 2001 and 943 in 2011, women were 48.5 per cent of the population in 2011, and Uttar Pradesh holds 16 per cent of India's people.

questions.q: True or False? 'Country Q's population structure diagram has a narrow base, a very wide middle and a top that is only slowly getting wider. By the chapter, this shows that Q already has an ageing population like Japan's.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. When the middle part is widest, most people are working adults and the chapter calls the population stable, like India's recent bell shape. An ageing population like Japan's has a wide top, with more older people than young adults.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: a widest middle means mostly working adults (a stable population); an ageing population has a wide top with more older people than young adults

questions.q:
Assertion (A): India's sex ratio improved between Census 2001 and Census 2011.
Reason (R): In 2011, women comprised 48.5 per cent of India's total population.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. A rests on the change from 933 to 943 females per 1,000 males; R is only a 2011 snapshot and says nothing about 2001 or why the ratio rose.

questions.q: Fig. 6.13 gives the share of India's population living in each state, in whole per cent, including Uttar Pradesh 16 per cent and Bihar 9 per cent; it does not say which year the shares are for. Fig. 6.5 gives India's population as 1,460 million in 2025 and 361 million in 1951. (a) Using the 2025 total, estimate the number of people in Uttar Pradesh. (b) Estimate the number in Bihar in the same way. (c) Compare the two states together with the whole of India in 1951. (d) Give two reasons why your answers to (a) and (b) are only estimates.
questions.a: (a) 16 per cent of 1,460 million = 233.6 million. (b) 9 per cent of 1,460 million = 131.4 million. (c) Together 233.6 + 131.4 = 365 million, which is slightly more than India's entire population of 361 million in 1951 (by about 4 million). (d) The shares in Fig. 6.13 are rounded to whole per cents, and Fig. 6.13 gives no year, so its shares may not belong to 2025, the year of the 1,460 million total.
s: (a) About 233.6 million in Uttar Pradesh
(b) About 131.4 million in Bihar
(c) Together about 365 million, a little more than all of India's 361 million in 1951
(d) Shares are rounded whole per cents, and Fig. 6.13 states no year, so they may not match the 2025 total

questions.q: The chapter calls a large young population the 'youth bulge'. Which age group does it give for this young population?
questions.a: 16 to 30 years.

questions.q: Fig. 6.17 gives the median age of the population as: India 28, Japan 50, Italy 48, Germany 47, China 40 and the USA 39 years. Which country's median age is closest to India's?
questions.a: The USA, whose median age of 39 is 11 years above India's 28; China's 40 is 12 years above.

questions.q: (a) What is a demographic dividend, as the chapter defines it? (b) Roughly what share of India's population is in the working-age group of 15 to 59 years?
questions.a: (a) The economic growth potential of a nation resulting from a younger and productive age structure. (b) Nearly 65 per cent.
s: (a) Economic growth potential arising from a younger, productive age structure
(b) Nearly 65 per cent

questions.q: Answer each part in a line. (a) Fig. 6.17 gives Italy's median age as 48 years and India's as 28 years. By how many years is Italy's median age higher? (b) Which two Indian states does the chapter name as already experiencing significant population ageing compared with Bihar and Uttar Pradesh? (c) The number of Indian children under five peaked in 2007 and the number of Indians under 15 peaked in 2011. How many years apart were the two peaks? (d) Japan faces a shortage of workers as its people grow older. Name one step the chapter says Japan has taken to deal with this. (e) Give one way, from the chapter, in which older people continue to contribute to their family and society after they withdraw from economic activities.
questions.a: (a) 48 - 28 = 20 years. (b) Kerala and Tamil Nadu. (c) 2011 - 2007 = 4 years. (d) Any one of: it has raised the retirement age; it has employed technology and automation to make up for labour shortages; it uses large-scale community centres, robots and AI assistants to help care for older adults. (e) Any one of: they share their knowledge and wisdom with family and society; they guide rituals and storytelling, so cultural continuity becomes possible; they hold knowledge that may not be in books.
s: (a) 20 years
(b) Kerala and Tamil Nadu
(c) 4 years
(d) One of Japan's steps: higher retirement age, technology and automation, community centres, robots or AI assistants
(e) One contribution of elders: sharing knowledge and wisdom, or guiding rituals and storytelling

questions.q: Sonpur (an illustrative town) has a very large number of people aged 20 to 35, but most of them cannot find work. (a) Explain the two ways in which, by the chapter, a working-age population helps a country grow when its people do work. (b) Using the chapter's meaning of demographic dividend, explain why Sonpur's young people are for now only a potential, and name one investment the chapter says developing countries need to turn it into growth.
questions.a: (a) First, young people who work in factories, offices or farms, or start businesses, increase the volume of economic activity, which helps the country grow. Second, working people earn money and pay taxes, which the government uses to build schools, hospitals, roads and parks. (b) The demographic dividend is a growth potential arising from a young, productive age structure; if the young people have no work, neither the economic activity nor the taxes follow, so the potential is not yet used. The chapter says developing countries must harness it through investment in good education, skilling and healthcare.
s: (a) Working young people raise the volume of economic activity (work or start businesses)
(a) They earn and pay taxes that the government uses for schools, hospitals, roads and parks
(b) Without work the dividend stays a potential; names education, skilling or healthcare as the needed investment

questions.q:
Consider the following statements.
I. By Fig. 6.17, India's median age of 28 years is 12 years lower than China's.
II. The youth bulge is common in countries at Stage 3 of demographic transition.
III. To deal with labour shortages, Japan has lowered its retirement age so that young people get jobs.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I only. China's median age is 40, so India's 28 is 12 years lower. The youth bulge is common at Stage 2, not Stage 3, and Japan has raised, not lowered, its retirement age.

questions.q:
A district in Tamil Nadu (illustrative figures) had 20 lakh people in 2011 and is expected to still have 20 lakh in 2031. In 2011, 12 per cent of its people were aged 60 and above and 66 per cent were aged 15 to 59. By 2031 these shares are expected to be 18 per cent and 60 per cent. The district has money for one large project: an elderly-care wing in the district hospital, or a skilling centre for young people.
(a) Find the number of people aged 60 and above in 2011 and in 2031.
(b) Find the number of people aged 15 to 59 for every person aged 60 and above, in each year.
(c) Name two pressures that the chapter says an ageing population creates.
(d) Which project would you fund first? Justify your choice using your answers and the chapter.
questions.a: (a) 12 per cent of 20 lakh = 2.4 lakh in 2011; 18 per cent of 20 lakh = 3.6 lakh in 2031. (b) 2011: 13.2 lakh / 2.4 lakh = 5.5 people aged 15 to 59 for each elderly person; 2031: 12 lakh / 3.6 lakh = about 3.3. (c) Any two of: pressure on healthcare systems because older adults need more healthcare; fewer workers to replace those who retire, which can slow the economy; difficulty paying pensions and providing services because of fewer young taxpayers. (d) Either choice can be justified. The elderly-care wing answers the 50 per cent rise in elderly people and the chapter's point that older adults need more healthcare. The skilling centre answers the fall in workers per elderly person from 5.5 to about 3.3: the chapter says developing countries must harness the dividend through education and skilling, so that fewer workers are more productive and pay the taxes that fund care.
s: (a) 2.4 lakh in 2011 and 3.6 lakh in 2031
(b) 5.5 in 2011 and about 3.3 in 2031
(c) Two of: pressure on healthcare, fewer workers to replace retirees, harder to pay pensions and provide services
(d) A justified choice that uses the computed figures and the chapter's reasoning

questions.q: Compare how the chapter says developed countries and developing countries must prepare for demographic transition, and analyse which of the two kinds of preparation India needs now. Use the median ages of Fig. 6.17 (India 28, Japan 50) and what the chapter says about when India's demographic window closes.
questions.a: Developed countries must support an ageing society while maintaining productivity and innovation: Japan, for example, has raised its retirement age, used technology and automation for labour shortages, and uses community centres, robots and AI assistants to care for older adults. Developing countries must harness the demographic dividend through investment in good education, skilling and healthcare, and help women join the workforce despite the double burden of job and household duties, through supportive family systems and childcare such as daycare centres. India, with a median age of 28 against Japan's 50, has a large working-age population now, so its first need is the developing-country task of harnessing the dividend. But the window is limited: the under-five population peaked in 2007, the under-15 population in 2011, and after 2050 India's population will begin to move towards an older one, with Kerala and Tamil Nadu already ageing. So India must use the dividend now while beginning to prepare for an older society.
s: Developed countries: support an ageing society while keeping productivity and innovation
Japan's measures: raised retirement age, technology and automation, community centres, robots or AI assistants
Developing countries: harness the dividend through education, skilling and healthcare
Women's double burden and the need for childcare such as daycare centres
Judgement for India: median age 28 means harness the dividend now, but the window closes after 2050 (peaks of 2007 and 2011, Kerala and Tamil Nadu ageing), so prepare for ageing too
